failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM651.924/925 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Wear (TSB LI80.20-P-050001)
items.whatHappens: The early OM651 timing chain tensioner can fail, leading to chain slack, a distinct metallic rattle on cold starts, and potentially catastrophic valve-to-piston contact if the chain jumps a tooth.
items.repairVsReplace: Mercedes issued an updated tensioner design to resolve this. If caught early, replacing the tensioner and chain is cost-effective. If valve damage has already occurred, a full reconditioned OM651 unit is required.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death")
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads, leading to a distinct tapping noise, rough idling, and a strong smell of exhaust in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: DPF and EGR Clogging
items.whatHappens: Urban driving patterns cause excessive soot buildup in the EGR valve and Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF), leading to restricted airflow, limp mode, and increased backpressure that can prematurely wear the turbocharger.
items.repairVsReplace: Professional DPF cleaning or EGR replacement is a standard repair. If the turbocharger has suffered damage from prolonged backpressure, a full turbo rebuild or replacement is necessary.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2011 units with the updated timing chain tensioner and revised ECU mapping show significantly fewer catastrophic chain failures, making them the most desirable examples of this engine family .

variants.title: OM651.924/925 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The OM651 family fragments into numerous raw sub-codes that share the same dominant failure story but differ critically by mounting orientation, chassis calibration, and emissions hardware. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting a transverse-spec engine into a longitudinal chassis (or vice versa) is physically impossible without extensive fabrication. - Fitted to: C-Class W204 (C 200 CDI), E-Class W212 (E 200 CDI) - Key technical difference: The standard longitudinal mounting variant for rear-wheel-drive saloons, featuring the traditional Mercedes engine bay layout and specific RWD bellhousing pattern. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; no unique widespread defects beyond the standard tensioner and seal issues. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the transverse .925 variant; the engine mounts, subframe, driveshaft interface, and wiring loom are entirely different. - Fitted to: A-Class W176 (A 200 CDI), B-Class W246 (B 200 CDI) - Key technical difference: The transverse mounting variant designed specifically for Mercedes' MFA front-wheel-drive platform. The accessory drive, oil sump, and transmission mating face are completely reconfigured for a transverse layout. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; transverse packaging makes the timing chain tensioner slightly more labour-intensive to access than in the longitudinal variants. - Interchange note: Cannot be swapped with the .924 under any circumstances; the physical orientation of the engine block and ancillary drives are mirrored. - Fitted to: C-Class W204 (C 200 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY), E-Class W212 (E 200 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY) - Key technical difference: Functionally identical to the .924 in core architecture, but calibrated with specific BlueEFFICIENCY emissions hardware, revised alternator management, and low-rolling-resistance ancillary drives. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Directly interchangeable with the .924 in most RWD applications, provided the ECU and specific emissions plumbing are swapped to match the original chassis specification. - Fitted to: GLK-Class X204 (GLK 200 CDI) - Key technical difference: The longitudinal variant calibrated specifically for the heavier GLK-Class SUV chassis, featuring revised cooling capacity, heavy-duty engine mounts, and specific 4MATIC integration points where applicable. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the heavier host vehicle can place slightly more thermal stress on the EGR cooler during urban use. - Interchange note: Requires matching heavy-duty mounts and specific 4MATIC transfer case plumbing; not a direct drop-in for a standard saloon without modification. - Fitted to: Select export W212 models and specific commercial chassis applications - Key technical difference: A longitudinal tune designed for specific regional emission standards or heavier gross vehicle weights, featuring a unique injection pump calibration and reinforced accessory brackets. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Directly interchangeable with the .924/.930 in most passenger car applications, provided the injection pump and ECU mapping are swapped to match the original chassis specification.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM651.924/925 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM651.924/925 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented replacement of the timing chain tensioner and injector seals. Given the catastrophic risk of chain failure, buying a used unit with unknown history is a significant financial risk.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM651 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by installing the updated timing chain tensioner, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR/DPF components, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM651 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage W212 E-Class or W204 C-Class hosts where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM651 engine is installed by specialists familiar with Mercedes CDI systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM651 is typically found in W204, W212, W176, and W246 vehicles valued between £5,000 and £18,000, a full replacement is generally financially viable and comfortably within the host vehicle's value . Replacement cost rarely exceeds the scrap threshold for these chassis, making a reconditioned unit a highly sensible investment.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM651.924/925 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain tensioner wear (addressed under TSB LI80.20-P-050001), injector seal weeping ("Black Death"), and DPF/EGR clogging. The timing chain tensioner can fail and cause catastrophic valve damage if ignored, while injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup but is a cheap preventative fix. items.answer: A reconditioned OM651.924/925 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaw by installing the updated timing chain tensioner, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR/DPF components, whereas a used engine with unknown history risks an immediate catastrophic chain failure. items.question: What is the difference between OM651.924, .925, .930, .940, and .950?
items.answer: The OM651.924 is the longitudinal saloon variant, the .925 is the transverse compact-car variant, the .930 is the BlueEFFICIENCY tune, the .940 is the longitudinal SUV variant, and the .950 is the export/commercial tune. They share the same core block, but the engine mounts, ECU mapping, and accessory drives differ significantly.
